strengths: Simple, training-free, closed-form idea (per-sequence FLD projection of ReID features conditioned on historical trajectories) that is intuitive and well-motivated by the observed mismatch between generic ReID objectives and the sequence-specific discrimination needs of MOT.

Strong and fairly extensive empirical validation: improvements on DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, and zero-shot transfer results on TAO with multiple visual backbones (MASA-R50/Detic/G-DINO/SAM-B), consistently showing gains over untransformed baselines.

Thoughtful ablations isolating each proposed component (FLD vs PCA projection, history length T, temporal-shifted centroid λ0, knowledge integration α), which helps substantiate that each piece contributes incrementally.
Good qualitative visualizations (Fig. 1, 3, 4) that intuitively support the claimed clustering/separation benefits of the FLD projection versus PCA/LDA.
The method is lightweight, model-agnostic, and could plausibly be combined with existing trackers as a plug-in improvement, which is practically appealing.

Honest discussion of limitations, including computational cost of eigen-decomposition and lack of GPU-accelerated generalized eigensolvers, plus the omission of motion cues in the current tracker design.
weaknesses: The baseline tracker ("FastReID-MOT") is deliberately stripped of motion cues, multi-stage matching, and other engineering commonly used in SOTA trackers; while this isolates ReID effects, it makes head-to-head comparisons against fully-optimized hybrid/motion trackers (DiffMOT, Deep OC-SORT, etc.) somewhat unfair or at least difficult to interpret as a like-for-like SOTA comparison, since those methods also incorporate additional cues the proposed tracker lacks.

The core algorithmic idea (Fisher Linear Discriminant projection) is a well-known classical technique; the novelty is primarily in the application-specific adaptation (temporal-shifted centroid, knowledge integration) rather than a fundamentally new method, and these design choices (EMA decay, α blending) are heuristic and dataset-tuned rather than derived from a principled analysis.

Several key hyperparameters (T, λ0, α) are tuned per dataset or empirically searched via grid search on validation data, and the paper does not discuss sensitivity/robustness across domains beyond the ablation on DanceTrack; it's unclear how much retuning is needed to transfer performance to new domains, partially undermining the 'training-free' and 'zero-shot' framing.

Class labels for FLD (trajectory identities) are themselves noisy 'pseudo-labels' generated online by the tracker; if identity switches/misallocations occur, especially early in a sequence or in crowded scenes, this could corrupt the projection matrix, and the paper offers only brief qualitative acknowledgment (Sec 3.4) without deeper empirical stress-testing of this failure mode.

The FLD-based projection matrix computation (via eigen-decomposition of S_W^{-1} S_B) needs to be recomputed as new trajectory data arrives; the paper reports a modest speed (22.7 FPS) and acknowledges CPU eigen-decomposition is a bottleneck, raising practical concerns for real-time deployment on more crowded scenes with many identities.

TAO results, which stress general/open-vocabulary tracking, show comparatively small improvements, and the explanation given (that categories are already well separated) is plausible but not rigorously validated with additional analysis (e.g. per-class breakdown or feature separability metrics).

The paper does not compare against more sophisticated learned metric-learning or domain-adaptation baselines beyond PCA, leaving open whether other simple training-free alternatives (e.g., whitening, other LDA variants, online triplet-based rescaling) might achieve similar gains, which would strengthen the specific justification for FLD as the chosen technique.

Reported SOTA comparisons mix different underlying detectors and settings across methods (e.g., Oracle vs YOLOX detections in ablations, different ReID backbones across baselines), which could affect the fairness/interpretability of magnitude comparisons, though this is partially addressed via careful footnoting.

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: general ReID feature spaces are misaligned with the MOT requirement of discriminating a small, sequence-specific set of similar targets, illustrated clearly with the t-SNE visualizations in Fig. 1/3/4.

The proposed solution (sequence-specific FLD projection using historical trajectory features as class conditions) is training-free, has a closed-form solution, and is simple to integrate into existing appearance-based association pipelines, which is appealing for practical adoption.

Extensive and carefully designed ablations (history length T, temporal-shifted centroid weight λ0, knowledge-integration coefficient α, and FLD vs. PCA comparison) convincingly isolate the contribution of each proposed component rather than relying on a single end-to-end number.

Strong empirical gains on DanceTrack and SportsMOT for a purely appearance-based tracker, reaching performance competitive with or exceeding motion- and hybrid-based state-of-the-art methods, which is a non-trivial result given the traditional dominance of motion cues in these benchmarks.

Zero-shot transfer experiments with multiple MASA-based ReID backbones (R50, Detic, G-DINO, SAM-B) show the method generalizes across feature sources without any retraining, strengthening the claim of broad applicability.

The paper is transparent about its simplified single-stage baseline design choice (to isolate ReID effects) and discusses concrete limitations, including inference-speed bottlenecks from CPU-bound generalized eigendecomposition and the lack of motion cues.
weaknesses: FLD relies on the online tracker's own historical ID assignments as class labels; if IDs are already confused (which is exactly the hard-case scenario the paper targets), the projection could reinforce mismatches. This risk is only briefly addressed via the knowledge-integration weighted sum, without a deeper analysis of failure modes or sensitivity to ID-switch-heavy sequences.

The improvement on TAO is comparatively small, and the paper's own explanation (targets are already well-separated in diverse-category scenes) suggests the method's benefit may be confined to scenarios with many visually similar objects of the same category, limiting the scope of the claimed generality.

The naive ReID-only baseline tracker used for comparison against motion- and hybrid-based SOTA methods, while useful for isolating the appearance signal, is not a standard/mainstream tracker design, making some cross-table comparisons (Tables 1-3) less of an apples-to-apples comparison with heavily engineered SOTA pipelines that jointly optimize motion and appearance.

Per-frame generalized eigendecomposition is reported to be the main runtime bottleneck (22.7 FPS on a capable GPU/CPU combo), and no scaling analysis is provided for denser scenes with many more simultaneous trajectories (e.g., MOT20-like crowds), leaving open questions about real-time applicability in more crowded settings.

The core technique (Fisher Linear Discriminant for discriminative subspace projection) is a well-established classical method; the novelty lies primarily in its application and the two tracking-specific modifications (temporal-shifted centroid, knowledge integration), which is a comparatively incremental technical contribution.

Table 3 contains some presentation ambiguity (duplicate rows for HAT-FastReID-MOT† with different numbers, and unclear demarcation of which settings use joint training with the validation set), which could confuse reproducibility of the exact reported SOTA comparison.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: MOT is a closed-set discrimination problem within a single video, not an open-set retrieval problem, and this is convincingly supported by a systematic correlation analysis (δ1000 vs AssA) on multiple datasets before proposing the method.
The proposed history-aware FLD transformation is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate into existing ReID-based and hybrid trackers, which is an attractive practical property.

Extensive and carefully designed experiments: ablations isolate the contribution of FLD vs. PCA, supervised vs. history-aware labeling, history length, temporal weighting, and knowledge-integration coefficient, providing solid evidence for each design choice.

Broad generalization tests across multiple ReID/visual backbones (FastReID, MASA with ResNet50/Detic/G-DINO/SAM), multiple trackers (ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Hybrid-SORT), and multiple datasets (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, MOT20, TAO) with consistent (if variable-sized) improvements.

Honest and thoughtful discussion of limitations, including reduced gains on hybrid-based trackers and MOT17/TAO, inference-speed overheads, and reporting of unsuccessful technical attempts, which strengthens scientific credibility.
Good reproducibility support via detailed appendix (hyperparameter settings, oracle setup, ablation configurations).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is the application of a classical, well-known technique (FLD/LDA) with dynamically defined labels from tracking history; the algorithmic novelty is modest, and the primary contribution is more conceptual/empirical than methodological.

Comparisons against very recent state-of-the-art trackers are explicitly omitted (acknowledged in Appendix D), which weakens the strength of some 'state-of-the-art' claims made in the abstract and results sections.

Improvements are inconsistent across settings: gains on MOT17, MOT20, TAO, and hybrid-based trackers are comparatively small, suggesting the method's benefit is highly dependent on how visually redundant/similar targets are within a video, limiting the generality of the claimed impact.

The added computational cost is significant (FPS roughly halved due to per-frame generalized eigenvalue decomposition), and the paper's own analysis shows this remains an open engineering problem, which may hinder real-time deployment despite claims of practicality.

The knowledge-integration step (linear fusion of original and transformed similarity scores) is a fairly ad hoc heuristic without deeper theoretical justification beyond intuitive trade-off arguments.

Reliability of the online-computed projection matrix under limited/noisy historical labels (e.g., few samples per new trajectory, occlusion-corrupted tracks) is only handled heuristically via score fusion rather than analyzed rigorously (e.g., no bound on estimation error or systematic study of failure cases from erroneous history labels).
Results are reported as single-run point estimates without variance/multiple seeds, so the statistical robustness of the reported gains is not established.
